results.message: Why did your bishops meet in councils?

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
We met in councils to judge what concerned us together, as bishops who would answer both to God and to one another. A question too large for one man, or one that pressed on many at once, brought us together. Cyprian opened the council of 256 with a rule that names how we understood ourselves: “None of us sets himself up as a bishop over other bishops, and none of us uses a tyrant's terror to force a colleague into obedience. Every bishop has his own right to judge, in keeping with the freedom and power allowed to him. He can no more be judged by another bishop than he himself can judge another. Instead, let us all wait for the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ. He is the only one who has the power both to place us in the government of His Church and to judge how we conduct ourselves there.”

Each bishop had his own right of judgment. No one forced a colleague to obey. Only Christ judges us. Yet we met, argued, and decided -- because a bishop answers not only for his own people but to the colleagues who sit beside him.

Augustine held councils accountable to something wider still. A small council yields to a wider one, and even the widest can be corrected when later experience brings to light what was hidden. We do not hide that this is a real disagreement between them, and we do not claim it was ever fully resolved. But both held that councils were real gatherings, with real authority, over real questions. The two formulas name different grounds for that authority. The fact of the councils themselves, and their binding force, neither bishop disputed.

names.name: Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop of Carthage (248/249-258)

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop, chosen while still new to the faith, over his own reluctance. During a plague he taught us to love even our enemies. He was put to death under Valerian.

dates.display: a trained rhetorician who turned from a public career to Christian life, converted c. 246; ordained and elected bishop of Carthage between roughly July 248 and April 249 by the acclamation of the Carthaginian people, over the recorded opposition of five presbyters, while still newly baptised, as his deacon Pontius tells it; banished to Curubis under the Valerianic persecution; executed under the emperor Valerian in 258

names.name: Augustinius of Hippo Regius, presbyter 391, bishop 395/396-430

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop at Hippo. The people seized him and brought him to be made a presbyter while he wept. Later they pressed him into the bishop's office over his own refusal. He spent his last days weeping over psalms of penitence, while an army lay outside the walls.

dates.display: converted 386, baptised 387; seized by the congregation at Hippo and ordained presbyter against his own wishes in 391, weeping through it (Possidius, Vita IV); designated coadjutor and consecrated bishop of Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia, in 395/396, again amid popular acclamation (Possidius, Vita VIII); died 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo
